# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

# The specification as HTML for a phone

`spec2html.py` converts the specification's LaTeX into a reader of static pages: the front matter, the 43 chapters and the 10 appendices, 54 pages. The pages go to `docs/specification/`, beside the revival page, and GitHub Pages serves them at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/ once `main` is pushed (`.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `docs/`). 3. Every table and display is compared with the PDF. "The checks" below says how, and what a person still has to look at.

3	# The specification as HTML for a phone
4	
5	`spec2html.py` converts the specification's LaTeX into a reader of static pages: the front matter, the 43 chapters and the 10 appendices, 54 pages. The pages go to `docs/specification/`, beside the revival page, and GitHub Pages serves them at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/ once `main` is pushed (`.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `docs/`). Nothing comes from another site.
6	
7	A first sample of 2026-11-10 held the front matter and chapters 1 to 6. The curator read it and decided how the rest is made; `curator-notes.md` holds his words. This run follows them:
8	
9	1. Examples and displays are LaTeX converted to SVG. The converter's own rendering of displayed code and formulas is gone.
10	2. Code words and formulas inside a sentence stay HTML text, with the three rules of `reader.css` that he approved (no ligatures in code, the inline highlight with narrow side padding, serif curly quotation marks). Those rules are unchanged.
11	3. Every table and display is compared with the PDF. "The checks" below says how, and what a person still has to look at.
12	4. An address of the authors' text gets the edition's link to the Internet Archive.
13	5. The revival's paragraph in the preface has the tint of the revival's additions, and the opening explains the tint.
14	6. A quote pair around the whole of a typewriter span is curly; an apostrophe inside code stays as typed.
15	7. Where the specification shows ASCII, the page shows ASCII.
16	
17	## The files
18	
19	- `spec2html.py`: the conversion and the site's pages. Python 3 with its standard library and `fontTools` (to read the fonts it makes). It runs `latex`, `dvisvgm` and Emacs (for the tree's Fortify).
20	- `reader.css`, `reader.js`: the reader. The build copies them into `docs/specification/`.
21	- `check.js`: the reader in Chromium at a phone's width (below).
22	- `compare.js`: every display in Chromium against LaTeX's own picture of it (below).
23	- `pdfcheck.py`: the words of every block against the words of `Specification/fortress.pdf` (below).
24	- `curator-notes.md`: the curator's decisions and notes.
25	
26	The build also writes `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/` under `docs/specification/`: the fonts of the displays.
27	
28	## Running it
29	
30	From the repository root:
31	
32	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --list            # every chapter with its slug
33	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try variables,functions
34	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try all
35	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py                   # the whole specification, into docs/specification/
36	
37	- A plain run takes about a minute when the work folder is warm, and about three minutes when it is empty. It rewrites every page of `docs/specification/`: the 54 chapter pages, `index.html` (the contents), `notes.html`, `references.html`, `reader.css`, `reader.js`, `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/`. No page is edited by hand.
38	- `--try` converts into the work folder only (`<work>/try/`, with the reader's files, so the pages can be opened) and prints, for each chapter, what did not convert. It writes nothing under `docs/`.
39	- `--chapters a,b` publishes only those chapters; a cross-reference into a chapter that is left out shows its number and "[not converted yet]".
40	- The script exits 1 if a published chapter holds a construct that it did not convert, a display on which LaTeX reported an error, or a display that uses a character that the fonts lack. Such a place shows in the page in red, and the report names it.
41	- `--work` sets the scratch folder (default `/tmp/spec-html-work`): the examples as Fortify renders them, the LaTeX file of each chapter's displays with its log, the SVGs, the fonts. `--base` sets the public address that the links of exported notes start with.
42	- The script reads `Specification/`, `SpecData/examples/`, `SpecData/tables/`, `Fortify/`, and the `.fsi` files of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`. It writes nothing in the original tree. It builds and runs no Fortress.
43	
44	## How the text is converted
45	
46	The script is a converter of its own over the macros that the chapters use (`pandoc` and `htlatex` were tried on the first sample: the first drops Fortify's markup without a word, the second stops under the tree's macros).
47	
48	- **Structure.** It walks the `\input`s from `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` and numbers parts, chapters, sections, subsections, figures, lemmas and theorems as LaTeX does. Each page is one chapter. A section's anchor is its label (`\seclabel{overview:apis}` gives `#sec-overview-apis`); a section without a label gets `#s-` and its title.
49	- **Running text** becomes HTML: paragraphs, lists, headings, footnotes, the authors' `\note` boxes ("Draft note"), the revival's `\revision` callouts. Fortify's markup and formulas inside a sentence become HTML text with Unicode characters, italics, superscripts and subscripts. The `\newcommand`s of `Specification/latex-common/macros/` are read and expanded, and so are the definitions that a chapter makes for itself (`\def`, `\newcommand`, `\renewcommand`, `\RenewDocumentCommand`), and the macro files that Appendix A reads for each of its calculi, in its order.
50	- **Displays** are set by LaTeX. A display is an example (`\begin{Fortress}`, or a file of `SpecData/examples/` that the tree's tool `foreg` renders, as the specification's `ant genSource` does), a displayed formula (`\[ \]`, `$$ $$`, `align`, `eqnarray`), a table (`tabular`, `array`), a grammar box (`Grammar`, `GrammarTwo`), a `tabbing` or `ttt` block, a drawing (`*.eepic`), and a table of reserved words (written as the build's Perl scripts write it). For each chapter the script writes one LaTeX file with the preamble of `fortress.tex` and one page for each display, in a box of the PDF's text width; the chapter's own definitions go into the file at their places; the labels of the whole specification go into its `.aux` file, so that a reference inside a display prints its number and links to its page. `latex` sets the file, `dvisvgm` converts each page, and the script puts the SVG into the page, inline.
51	  - The text of a display is SVG text in the TeX fonts, so it can be selected and copied. The fonts are made by dvisvgm from the fonts of the TeX installation and are served from `fonts/`; a page loads only those that it shows.
52	  - One SVG serves the light and the dark theme: its ink is `currentColor`, the colour of the text around it.
53	  - A display wider than the screen scrolls sideways inside its frame, at the PDF's proportions: a display is not reflowed.
54	  - A footnote inside a display joins the chapter's footnotes, and the display shows its number.
55	  - An example that has a source form shows it too, as before: the lines between `(** EXAMPLE **)` and `(** END EXAMPLE **)` of the `.fss` file, or the commented lines that the authors left before `\begin{Fortress}`. A switch above an example changes all examples.
56	- **A formula inside a sentence that HTML text cannot show** (an array, an overstruck operator, a binomial, a command that the converter does not know) is set by LaTeX too, as an SVG on the line's baseline. There are 83 of them, most in chapters 16 and 34 and Appendix A. Every other inline formula is HTML text, as the curator decided.
57	- **The API listings of the library** (chapters 29 and 30) are made as the build makes them: the tree's tool `fortex` on a copy of each `.fsi` file. Their code is set by LaTeX, their documentation comments are running text. They show the library as it is in the tree today.
58	- **Cross-references** are links. **Citations** show the key of the work and link to `references.html`.
59	
60	## The edition's layer over the authors' text
61	
62	The source text is not changed for any of this; the converter adds it, and it is visible as the edition's.
63	
64	- **The tint.** What the 2026 revival added stands on a light tint of the ground (`.rv` and `aside.revision` in `reader.css`, the colour `--rev-bg`, in light and in dark): the callout of a revised passage, the revival's paragraph in the preface, the revival's section of Appendix I, and the links below. The contents page and the preface open with one sentence that shows the tint and says what it means. The converter knows the revival's paragraph and section from two short lists at its top, `REVIVAL_PARAGRAPHS` and `REVIVAL_SECTIONS`: the source does not mark them.
65	- **Archived copies.** Beside each address of the authors' text (`http://projectfortress.sun.com` and the others, also in the references), the edition puts a link "archived copy" to `https://web.archive.org/web/2008/<address>`. The Internet Archive resolves a partial date to the nearest capture. 2008 is the year of the release that the preface names with the address; `ARCHIVE` at the top of the script sets it. The container cannot reach the Internet Archive, so no link was opened.
66	- Not built, because the curator has not decided it: marking which words of a revised passage changed (`curator-notes.md`, "The revival's callouts do not show which text changed").
67	
68	## The reader
69	
70	- **Place.** A chapter page stores, in `localStorage` under `fortress-spec.place.v1`, the block at the top of the screen, for each chapter and for the last one read. The start page offers to continue there; a chapter opened from the contents offers the place where that chapter was left.
71	- **Notes.** The pencil at the end of a paragraph, in the bar of a code example, under a table or beside a heading opens a text box under that place. `notes.html` lists all notes, exports them as text, and imports such a text. They are kept under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`.
72	- **Without storage** (private browsing) the pages work, a note lasts until the page is left, and a warning says so.
73	- **Select.** The button beside a heading selects that section's text up to its first subsection, for Speak.
74	
75	### The ids that notes hang on
76	
77	- The id of a paragraph is a hash of its words (`#p-934d16e7`). Every paragraph of the first sample keeps its id, among them the two that carry the curator's notes, `preface.html#p-0ea553b6` and `preface.html#p-033235cb`. To keep them, the hash still counts the words "[not converted yet]" after a reference into a chapter outside the first sample, as that sample showed them; the edition's own links are not counted.
78	- One paragraph of chapter 4 changed its id, because its words changed: the one with a quote pair inside a typewriter span (decision 6). 
79	- The ids of tables (`t-`), grammar boxes (`g-`), and code blocks without a source form (`c-`) changed: 34 in the first sample's chapters (14 in chapter 2, 12 in chapter 4, 2 in chapter 5, 6 in chapter 6). They were hashes of the HTML that the converter's own rendering made, which is gone; they are now hashes of the display's LaTeX source. A code block with a source form keeps its id. `reader.js` keeps a note whose place is gone and lists it at the top of its chapter, with the words it was written on.
80	
81	## Changes to reader.css and reader.js
82	
83	For a page that uses the reader's files, such as the walk-through under `docs/microgpt/`:
84	
85	- `reader.js` is unchanged.
86	- No rule of `reader.css` was changed or removed, and no class was renamed.
87	- Added to `reader.css`, at its end: `svg.tx` and `svg.tx.il` (a display, and one inside a sentence), `.mw` (the frame of a long formula inside a sentence), `.rv`, `a.ed`, `.legend` (the edition's layer), `.doc` (the documentation text of an API listing), `.hr` (a rule inside a formula), and `white-space: normal` for `.m` inside headings, `dt`, `figcaption`, `summary` and `nav`.
88	- The converter no longer writes these, whose rules stay in the stylesheet: `.fx-r .tb`, `.fx-r .l`, `.gapline`, `.cm`, `table.tab`, `table.grammar`, `div.words`, `.tw.gr .label`. `.fx-r`, `.dm` and `.tw` now hold one `svg.tx`.
89	- A chapter page with displays links `tex-fonts.css` and carries a `<style>` with the font classes of its SVGs (`svg.tx text.t0` and so on).
90	
91	## The checks
92	
93	Serve the pages, then run the three:
94	
95	    mkdir -p /tmp/spec-srv && ln -sfn "$PWD/docs" /tmp/spec-srv/fortress
96	    python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/spec-srv &
97	    node explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/check.js
98	    node explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/compare.js /tmp/spec-html-work http://localhost:8765/fortress/specification/
99	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/pdfcheck.py
100	
101	- **`check.js`** (about a minute) opens every page that the contents lists at 390 px, light and dark. It fails on a page that scrolls sideways, on a construct left unconverted, on a display whose font is missing or lacks a character, and if the ink of the displays is not the colour of the text in both themes. It checks that the text of a display can be selected, the three rules for code inside a sentence, the curly quote pair, the two note-carrying ids of the preface, the archive link, and the tint. Then, as before: notes on a paragraph, a code example and a heading, the place, export and import, the switch between the two forms of the code, Select, that no request leaves the site, and the pages without `localStorage`. It saves two screenshots.
102	- **`compare.js`** (about five minutes) sets each chapter's displays a second time, with `pdflatex` from the same file, makes a picture of each page with `pdftoppm`, takes a picture of the same display in Chromium, and compares the two: their sizes, and the share of the ink of each that lies within two pixels of the other's. This is the check that would have caught the chapter 4 tables of the first sample. It found two faults while this run was built: dvisvgm wrote the Courier font without the characters U+002E to U+005F when it wrote the whole font at once (the fonts are now written in pieces of 32 codes, and the build reads each piece back and fails if a character that a display uses is missing), and the frame of a table lost its top and left lines at the edge of the picture (each SVG now has a margin).
103	- **`pdfcheck.py`** (ten seconds) reduces every paragraph, heading, list item, caption and display of the pages to its letters and digits, does the same with the text of `Specification/fortress.pdf`, and looks for each block's runs of ten characters in the PDF. A block that lost a row, was set from the wrong source or was filled with something else fails. It found the lemma numbers of Appendix B, the lost footnotes of grammar boxes, and four commands that the text form had mishandled (`\rule`, `\vspace*`, `\not` before a macro, and the calculi's own `\exp`).
104	
105	Results of 2026-11-13, on the 54 pages:
106	
107	- `check.js`: all pass.
108	- `compare.js`: 1,229 displays compared, 5 differ, none by a fault of the page. Three of chapter 16 agree to 77–92 % where the limit is 92 % (one small glyph, and a row of typewriter symbols that the two renderers hint differently). One of chapter 23 holds a citation and one of chapter 33 a reference, which the reader shows as a key and a link and the second LaTeX run shows as `?`.
109	- `pdfcheck.py`: 6,845 blocks compared, 8 not found in the PDF, each with 63–75 % of its runs where the limit is 75 %: three paragraphs and five displays dense with symbols (chapters 9, 13, 16, 40 and Appendix F), read and found right. 98 more are displays of symbols with too few letters to judge by words; `compare.js` covers them.
110	
111	What these checks do not do, and what was looked at by eye:
112	
113	- No tool here places a display beside its page of the PDF. `compare.js` compares with LaTeX's picture from the same source and macros as the PDF, and `pdfcheck.py` compares words with the PDF. Together they cover every display, but neither is a person looking at the PDF's page.
114	- Looked at beside the PDF's page, at 390 px and at a desktop's width: the preface; the character tables of chapter 4 (page 45 of the PDF, the curator's example: the `&`, the row, and the white brackets are right) and its reserved words (page 51); the grammar boxes of sections 7.1 and 9.5 (page 96); Figure 16.1 (page 172); Figure 22.1 (page 228); the first two figures of Appendix A (page 506); sections F.2 to F.4 of Appendix F (page 547).
115	- Not looked at beside the PDF by a person: the other displays and tables, among them most of the 979 rows of the operator tables of Appendix F, the inference rules of Appendix A apart from the first figure, and the API listings.
116	
117	## What differs from the PDF
118	
119	| What | Where | Why |
120	|---|---|---|
121	| A display does not reflow | every chapter | It is LaTeX's page at the PDF's width; on a phone a wide one scrolls inside its frame. |
122	| Formulas inside a sentence are HTML text in the device's fonts | every chapter | The curator's decision. Brackets do not stretch, spacing is the browser's, a fraction is two short lines. |
123	| Some symbols of a display copy as private-use characters | displays with `⟦ ⟧`, `⊢`, primes, large delimiters and other glyphs that the TeX fonts name without a Unicode value | dvisvgm gives such a glyph a code point from U+E000. The picture is right; a copy of the text, and Speak, get a character without meaning. |
124	| The bibliography's numbers | every `\cite`, also inside displays | The PDF numbers the cited works; the reader cites by key, `[JLS]`, and `references.html` lists every entry of `fortress.bib` under its key. |
125	| The index | every `\index` | Dropped; the reader has no index page. |
126	| The arrowheads of the five drawings are solid | chapter 22 | The PDF is made by pdflatex with `eepicemu`, which cannot fill; the reader's drawings come from `latex` with `eepic`, which fills them as the drawing asks. |
127	| Figures and tables stay where their source is | every chapter | None floats to the top of a page. |
128	| A display inside a draft note has the size of the text | a few notes | In the PDF the note's box sets it smaller, in the sans face. |
129	| The API listings show today's library | chapters 29 and 30 | They are made from the `.fsi` files of the tree, as the build makes them; a listing has no source form in the reader. |
130	| The page numbers of `\pageref` | rare | The reader has no pages. |
131	| The title page and the table of contents | front | The contents page of the reader stands for both. |
132	| Appendix I's section of the revival is tinted as a whole | Appendix I | The edition's layer. |

Answered at 17:4x from the tree: the parser reads a radix as digits or as a word (`parser/Literal.rats:102-109`, `RadixNames`; `nodes_util/NodeUtil.java:1251-1280`, `radix2Number`), the team's `tests/NumeralTest.fss:18-25` asserts `f_SIXTEEN + 2` is 17 and `DEAD.BEEF_16 = DEAD.BEEF_SIXTEEN`, and the static numerals carry the radix as a number, so the spelling is gone after the parser.
190	
191	### His question on the quotation marks (18:3x UTC on 2026-11-10)
192	
193	He saw a backtick and a straight apostrophe in the reader where the PDF has curly single quotes, and asked whether the source holds them or the converter makes them. Found: the LaTeX source writes every single quote as a backtick and an apostrophe, and LaTeX draws the pair as curly quotes. The converter makes the same change in running text. It leaves the pair as typed where the team wrote it inside a typewriter span, as in `\txt{`FBAB'}` at `Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:866`, while LaTeX's typewriter font draws it curly there too. Three places in the published pages, all in the chapter on lexical structure. For the reader's next run: a quote pair that wraps the whole content of a typewriter span becomes curly quotes; an apostrophe inside code stays as typed.
194	
195	### His rule on typography near the source (18:3x UTC on 2026-11-10)
196	
197	With two screenshots of rule 2 on enclosers (the reader and the PDF), he said the reader was hard to read there and the PDF easier, and: "we should keep it as close as possible to the original source, right? We can modernize" but "we should be careful what font are we using for the source code"; the house style's code font has ligatures, which he likes for the house style, "but here we need to be careful when it renders differently in a way that it hides the ASCII part. And converts stuff to Unicode rendering when the point is to show the ASCII."
198	
199	Done in `reader.css` at once, checked in a browser on that passage: code inside a sentence first lost its box and padding (the box came back, see below), so the quotation marks sit close; ligatures are off wherever code is shown; the curly quotation marks alone come from a serif face (a font face limited to U+2018 to U+201F, from fonts already on the device), since a sans face draws them like straight ticks. The three changes are the coordinator's choices under his rule. On seeing the browser picture he said of the first: "you lost The color highlight. I want that back in." So inline code keeps its highlight, with side padding cut to a tenth of an em.

# Earlier editions of the Fortress Language Specification

Two editions that Sun Microsystems published before version 1.0, kept here as the documents they are. Only their PDFs are known to survive in public; their LaTeX sources have not been found.

- `fortress.1.0alpha.pdf`: *The Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0 α*, 19 September 2006, 411 pages. Fetched on 2026-11-10 from https://psc.informatik.uni-jena.de/languages/HPCS/fortress-1.0alpha.pdf. sha256 `93d7edd59a12ac01d68409d310d6cdd5cebeae3a2d9f1f7d09d7932182b0e24b`.
- `fortress.1.0beta.pdf`: *The Fortress Language Specification, Version 1.0 β*, 6 March 2007, 441 pages. Fetched on 2026-11-10 from https://web.cs.ucla.edu/~palsberg/course/cs239/papers/fortress1.0beta.pdf. sha256 `8f275267c3992a90a6925d5d5100a5d8e0b656e910a79caccc3d43424d751ead`.

Both name as authors Eric Allen, David Chase, Joe Hallett, Victor Luchangco, Jan-Willem Maessen, Sukyoung Ryu, Guy L. Steele Jr. and Sam Tobin-Hochstadt, with Joao Dias, Carl Eastlund, Christine Flood, Yossi Lev and Cheryl McCosh as additional contributors. Each title page carries "© Sun Microsystems, Inc." and its date; neither file holds a licence statement. They are included at the repository owner's decision of 2026-11-10, unchanged, for the record of how the language's design moved.

The later editions are elsewhere in this repository:

- Version 1.0, 31 March 2008: `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, the PDF that the team released with the interpreter (the repository's tag `1.0`).
- The working draft as the team left it, 2 February 2011: the LaTeX sources in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`.
- The revival's revision of that draft: `Specification/`.

<!-- Leads on the earlier editions of the Fortress specification, for the curator's idea of showing the specification at its milestones: what an outside search of 2026-11-10, run by the curator, found, what this repository's git confirms, and what is still missing. Kept by the coordinating session. Nothing here was fetched into the tree. -->

# The specification's earlier editions: leads

## The editions and where a copy is

- **1.0α, 2006-09-19.** A PDF at the University of Jena: https://psc.informatik.uni-jena.de/languages/HPCS/fortress-1.0alpha.pdf (the curator's search; not opened from this container).
- **1.0β, 2007-03-06.** A PDF at UCLA: https://web.cs.ucla.edu/~palsberg/course/cs239/papers/fortress1.0beta.pdf (the same search); cited in papers as a Sun Microsystems technical report of 2007.
- **1.0, 2008-03-31.** `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` in this tree; the tag `1.0` (`0e8ede7e7f`) holds it as `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf` and no LaTeX. The search also found it on Sam Tobin-Hochstadt's site, and a post of 2008-04-05 that names the release archive `fortress-1.0.zip`; a report of June 2008 gives release 1.0 as Subversion changeset 1450.
- **The working draft, to 2011-02-02.** LaTeX in this tree: `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, byte for byte the team's `Specification/` of that day (F-163). The LaTeX entered the repository on 2009-10-20 and 2009-11-05 (`5da7257089`, `d26c347121`, Sukyoung Ryu). Its `fortress/preamble.tex:130-146` keeps the 1.0 release's preface as a comment.
- **The revival's text.** `Specification/`.

## Confirmed in this tree on 2026-11-10

- The public repository of 2008 was Subversion, not Mercurial: the tag's `README.txt` opens "PROJECT FORTRESS SUBVERSION REPOSITORY" and gives `svn checkout https://projectfortress.sun.com/svn/Community/trunk PFC`; its `.hgignore` lists `.svn`. The coordinator's lead of 16:5x, that it was a Mercurial repository, was wrong.
- The tag's `README.txt` describes `SpecData/` as the machine-readable files and examples of the specification; the specification's LaTeX is not in that snapshot.

## Not found

- The LaTeX sources of 1.0α, 1.0β and 1.0. The search's reading, and the coordinator's: they were kept outside the public trunk until 2009.

## Where to look next, from the search

- An inventory of the Internet Archive's captures of `projectfortress.sun.com` (`/Projects/Community/downloads/`, `/Projects/Community/browser/trunk/`, `/svn/Community/`) and of `research.sun.com/projects/plrg/`; release archives named `fortress-1.0.zip` or `fortress_*.zip`. This container cannot reach the Internet Archive.
- The authors: Sukyoung Ryu, whose commits brought the LaTeX in, and Sam Tobin-Hochstadt, who hosts the 1.0 PDF. A draft letter to Prof. Ryu is `explorations/coordinator/ryu-letter-2026-11-10-draft.md`.

## The two PDFs, fetched on 2026-11-10, in the tree since that day

Fetched at 17:4x UTC into the session's scratchpad, both whole and readable:

- 1.0α: 411 pages, 2,356,414 bytes, made 2006-09-19 (`pdfinfo`), sha256 `93d7edd59a12ac01d68409d310d6cdd5cebeae3a2d9f1f7d09d7932182b0e24b`.
- 1.0β: 441 pages, 1,975,153 bytes, made 2007-03-06, sha256 `8f275267c3992a90a6925d5d5100a5d8e0b656e910a79caccc3d43424d751ead`.

Each title page names the same eight authors (Allen, Chase, Hallett, Luchangco, Maessen, Ryu, Steele, Tobin-Hochstadt) and five additional contributors, and carries "© Sun Microsystems, Inc." with its date. Neither holds a licence statement anywhere in its text. The 1.0 PDF in the tree carries the same notice and no licence either; the team itself put it into the repository whose `LICENSE` is the BSD licence of 2007. The curator asked for the two to be committed and linked from the README; told of the missing licence, he confirmed it ("I am doing this."). They are in `Specification-history/`, with a README on where they came from, and `README.md` links to them there. `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is not the place for them: it is kept byte for byte equal to the team's working draft (F-163).

Sam Tobin-Hochstadt's public page (https://samth.github.io/) gives him as a professor of computer science at Indiana University, with the address samth@iu.edu.

## Where the editions were published, from the git history (added at 18:0x UTC on 2026-11-10)

- The history starts on 2007-01-04 (`72ae6881b1`); `b3d64f3261` of 2007-01-05 merges the licences into one file.
- No `.pdf`, `.ps` or `.tex` file is added before 2008-03-31, when `403afbe0b9` adds `Specification/fortress.1.0.pdf`. The tree of 2007-03-10 (`5ee788b346`) holds only `ProjectFortress/`, and in it a `.hgignore` file.
- `ProjectFortress/README` in that tree sends readers to `http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/fortress.pdf` for the specification, to `http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/` for other materials, and has a section "SYNTAX CHANGES SINCE FORTRESS LANGUAGE SPECIFICATION v.1.0 ALPHA".
- So 1.0α (2006-09-19) is earlier than the opened code and 1.0β (2007-03-06) is later, and both were published as a PDF on the research group's site, not in this history. One address served the current edition, so the Internet Archive's captures of that address, by date, are the place to look for each edition and for the drafts before 1.0α. Not checked from here: the archive is blocked in this container; whether the public Subversion server held folders other than `Community/trunk`.
